meta.ogDescription: An anecdote with no owner. The 1922 telling credits Rockefeller with other words; this exact sentence first appears in a 1926 book, attached to J. P. Morgan.

answer.label: Not Rockefeller — an anecdote that changed hands
answer.authorDates: Unattributed anecdote · in print by October 1922
answer.sourceLine: Nobody is documented as having said this. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the story to the Wall Street Journal in October 1922, where the reply is the shorter ‘I think they will fluctuate’ and the teller is Henry Poor — who had died in 1905, years before the article appeared. The sentence people quote today, with ‘the market’ in it, does not turn up until 1926, and there the speaker is J. P. Morgan.

source.excerpt: Young man, I believe the market is going to fluctuate.
trail: The earliest instance Quote Investigator located ↗ is an anecdote printed in the Wall Street Journal in October 1922 and credited to Henry Poor, the founder of the firm that became Standard & Poor’s. QI points out the obvious problem in its own words: Poor “died in 1905 several years before the article presenting the tale was published.” In that version the question is about Standard Oil securities and the answer is ‘I think they will fluctuate.’

After that the story simply changes hands. QI records it credited to Rockefeller again in the Washington Post in 1924, to J. P. Morgan in Laurence H. Sloan’s 1926 book Security Speculation: The Dazzling Adventure — which is where our exact sentence first appears — to Rockefeller once more in 1927, to William Rockefeller in 1928, and by 1934 to J. Pierpont Morgan, Jay Gould or Jesse Livermore depending on who was telling it the full chronology ↗.

Wikiquote is worth checking against this, because it shows how the line settled. Its J. P. Morgan page ↗ carries only the four-word form, “It will fluctuate”, cited to Jean Strouse’s Morgan: American Financier (Random House, 1999), p. 11 — not the longer sentence in circulation. Its John D. Rockefeller page ↗ has no fluctuate entry at all, in any section. So the credit this wording arrives with — Rockefeller — is the one Wikiquote does not connect to the remark at all.
source.cutTag: Laurence H. Sloan, Security Speculation: The Dazzling Adventure, 1926
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest appearance Quote Investigator locates for the wording people actually quote — and the speaker is Morgan, not Rockefeller. Four years earlier the same joke had been told about Rockefeller in different words and about a different subject: not the stock market at large, but Standard Oil’s own securities, which was a thing he genuinely knew from the inside. QI notes the story had to be altered once it moved to Morgan, who had no special knowledge of Standard Oil.

author.name: John D. Rockefeller
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Rockefeller
author.bio: John Davison Rockefeller Sr. (1839–1937) founded Standard Oil in 1870 and became the defining American industrialist of his age, later giving away a fortune through the foundations, universities and medical institutes that still carry his name. He attracts market wisdom he never uttered for a simple reason: a man that rich is assumed to have had a system, and a one-line system is exactly what this anecdote offers. The tell is that the same joke has been told about at least four other financiers.

misattribution.heading: Whose line is it, then?
misattribution.intro: In the space of forty years this joke was told about at least five different financiers. That is the signature of a floating anecdote rather than a remembered remark.

items.who: John D. Rockefeller, via a dead witness
items.why: The Wall Street Journal ran it in October 1922 as a story told by Henry Poor. Poor died in 1905, so the anecdote reached print through a narrator who could not be asked about it QI on the 1922 item ↗.

Laurence H. Sloan’s Security Speculation: The Dazzling Adventure gives the sentence quoted on this page. Because Morgan had no inside knowledge of Standard Oil, the question had to be broadened from those securities to the market in general — the alteration that produced the modern line QI on the 1926 item ↗.

items.who: William Rockefeller, Jay Gould, Jesse Livermore
items.why: QI records the remark handed to William Rockefeller in 1928 and, by 1934, to J. Pierpont Morgan, Jay Gould or Jesse Livermore in the same newspaper item. A saying that fits five different men equally well belongs to none of them the chronology ↗.

Wikiquote gives Morgan only “It will fluctuate”, cited to Jean Strouse’s biography, p. 11. The longer sentence in circulation is not what it records, and its Rockefeller page does not carry the remark at all Wikiquote on Morgan ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: No documentary evidence puts this sentence in Rockefeller’s mouth, or in Morgan’s. The earliest telling is second-hand from a man seventeen years dead, and the wording quoted today was first printed about a different financier entirely Quote Investigator’s account ↗.

context.heading: Why it keeps getting retold
lead: The joke works because it is a refusal dressed as an answer. Someone wants a tip; the great man gives a statement that is completely true, completely useless, and impossible to argue with. It flatters the teller and deflates the asker in one move, which is why it has survived a century of being reassigned.

It also explains why it drifts. The humour does not depend on who says it, only that he is rich enough for the question to make sense. Any sufficiently famous financier will do — and over forty years, most of them got a turn.
context.pull: A saying that fits five different men equally well belongs to none of them.
